Information since September points to a still-strong labor market and moderate growth, with robust household spending, but persistent weakness in business fixed investment and exports alongside inflation running below 2%. The literature emphasizes that investment shortfalls often account for slowdowns in real GDP and can weigh on future productive capacity, while expected inflation plays a key role in driving actual inflation dynamics (New Keynesian Phillips curve). Given evidence that monetary policy affects real activity in the short run (e.g., Sims’s VARs; B. Friedman; McCallum and Nelson), the FOMC’s 25 bp cut to 1.50–1.75% and steps to maintain ample reserves should provide some cyclical support. Open-economy research (Lane; Engel) also underscores that global conditions can transmit through trade and financial channels, consistent with soft exports. Net assessment: cautiously supportive tone due to policy easing and strong labor/consumption, tempered by capex weakness and muted inflation expectations.
